name: CO2 laser perioral rejuvenation

lead: CO2 laser resurfacing is a clinic treatment people choose to soften the vertical lines around the mouth and lips and give the area smoother, fresher-looking skin.

The laser emits at 10,600 nm, vaporises thin layers of skin and heats the deeper dermis, which prompts collagen and elastin renewal as the skin heals. Several trials are registered for perioral wrinkles, including a completed fractional CO2 study of 35 participants.

paras: A clinician treats the perioral area in a single clinic session, sometimes with a fractional (partial-coverage) setting. Patients plan for a healing period of redness and peeling afterward, and results build over the following weeks and months as collagen remodels. It is often discussed alongside other lip-area options such as fillers.

Described risks include hypopigmentation (lighter patches), scarring and herpes outbreaks around the mouth. Pigment and scarring risk is higher than with erbium lasers. It is a medical procedure performed by a clinician, and people with a history of cold sores are usually asked about it beforehand.

web.title: Europe PMC search: CO2 laser perioral wrinkles

angle.text: Patients get clinic CO2 laser resurfacing to smooth lines around the mouth and lips. The laser heats the deep skin layers, collagen and elastin renew as the skin heals, and the lines look softer over the following weeks. Trials are registered for perioral wrinkles.

lead: CO2 laser perioral rejuvenation uses a carbon dioxide laser to treat the vertical lines and fine wrinkles around the mouth, often called lipstick lines or smoker's lines. People have it done in a clinic to smooth the skin around the lips and upper lip so the lower face looks younger and the lip border more defined. CO2 lasers emit at 10,600 nm, vaporise thin layers of tissue and heat the deep dermis, which is thought to stimulate new collagen and elastin [1].

Perioral wrinkles are among the areas treated in the earliest published CO2 resurfacing series from the mid-1990s. Those studies reported large photographic improvements, with erythema lasting weeks to months as the main trade-off, and the technique has since evolved toward fractional systems that treat only a fraction of the skin at a time [1][2]. Registered trials also cover fractional CO2 and other lasers for perioral lines [3][4][5].
infobox: Erythema reported 1-6 months in early series [2][2]

paras: CO2 lasers were the first lasers used for resurfacing, and are used for deep wrinkles and sun damage; erbium and CO2 fractional systems are described as having a better safety profile than older lasers [1]. Perioral lines are a common target because the skin there is thin and repeated lip movement makes lines persist.

Laser skin resurfacing was first done with CO2 lasers: Wikipedia credits Thomas L. Roberts III with inventing the technique in the 1990s, citing a 1995 presentation, and says full-face resurfacing was first performed with a CO2 laser [1]. Ablative systems vaporise tissue, such as the 10,600 nm CO2 and 2940 nm Er:YAG lasers, whereas non-ablative systems leave the skin intact [1]. Fractional photothermolysis, introduced later, delivers many microscopic columns of heat and leaves healthy skin between them, which shortens healing; Fraxel is one such device [1].

Heating the deep dermis stimulates fibroblasts to form new collagen and elastin, which can improve skin thickness and firmness [1]. CO2 laser energy is strongly absorbed by water in tissue, producing vaporisation of the surface layer and a zone of coagulation beneath it. Wikipedia attributes the higher hypopigmentation and scarring risk of CO2 compared with erbium lasers to the heat and coagulation produced at the CO2 wavelength [1].

Hypopigmentation and scarring are noted with CO2 resurfacing, and acne and herpes outbreaks were observed in a 2008 study of 961 fractional treatments [1]. In the 1995 series of 47 patients, erythema lasted 1 to 6 months in every patient, and other events included contact dermatitis, transient hyperpigmentation, milia, one herpes simplex infection needing intravenous treatment and minor focal atrophy in one patient [2]. In a 259-patient series, erythema lasted 1 to 3 months and 30 percent had transient postinflammatory hyperpigmentation lasting about 3 months on average, with no scarring [2].

Early series reported results with pulsed CO2 lasers. In a 1996 study in Archives of Dermatology, four blinded reviewers scored photographs of 73 perioral and 38 periorbital sites treated with multi-pass pulsed CO2 laser; mean wrinkle score reductions were 2.34 for perioral and 2.25 for periorbital sites on a nine-point scale over 1 to 12 months, with transient erythema, postinflammatory hyperpigmentation and one hypertrophic scar [2].

A prospective series of 259 patients (104 perioral) treated with a high-energy pulsed CO2 laser reported average improvement of about 90 percent across areas on blinded assessment at up to 24 weeks, with the lowest response, 86.8 percent, in severe lines and glabellar lines caused by muscle movement [2]. A 1995 retrospective review of 47 patients treated with a char-free CO2 laser reported good to excellent results in all areas [2]. A randomised side-by-side comparison in 13 patients found one-pass CO2 and multiple-pass Er:YAG resurfacing gave similar wrinkle reduction and thermal injury, with less erythema at CO2 sites at 2 weeks [2].

ClinicalTrials.gov lists a completed fractional CO2 trial for perioral rhytides (35 participants) [3], a completed laser spot treatment trial (30 participants) [4], and a recruiting trial of a 2910 nm laser for perioral lines [5]. Separate physiology studies used CO2 laser pulses around the mouth to study pain reflexes, not rejuvenation [6].

timeline.event: Char-free CO2 laser resurfacing series reported in 47 patients [2]; Wikipedia cites a 1995 presentation for the technique [1].
Pulsed CO2 laser series reported for perioral and periorbital wrinkles [2][2].
